options: Permanent storage of files after shutdown
Fast short-term memory for programs running right now
Translating Python into machine code
Connecting the computer to the internet
computers.why: RAM holds whatever is running right now and is wiped when power goes off. Files that must survive a restart live in storage.

computers.q: What does the operating system do?
options: It is the chip that carries out every instruction
It is the text file where your code is saved
It manages hardware, files and running programs for other software
It is the Python library that reads CSV files
computers.why: The OS starts first and manages memory, files and processes so other programs can run. The CPU is hardware, not the OS.

computers.q: A customer runs your .py file on a server and gets 'command not found: python'. What is the most likely cause?
options: No Python interpreter is installed or on the PATH
The file needs to be compiled to .exe first
The server has too little RAM for the script
The CPU cannot read text files
computers.why: A .py file is just text; it needs the Python interpreter to run it. The error says the shell cannot find that program.

computers.q: Your script builds a list of 10,000 cleaned orders, then ends. The customer asks where the results are. What went wrong?
options: The CPU deleted the list to save power
The list was never saved to a file, so it vanished with the process
Python only keeps lists for one hour
The OS moved the list to the recycle bin
computers.why: Variables live in RAM and disappear when the program ends. To keep results you must write them to storage, such as a CSV file.

computers.q: A teammate says: 'I edited the script, so the new logic is already running on the server.' What is the mistake?
options: Scripts must be run twice before changes apply
Nothing is wrong; edits apply instantly
Only compiled languages need saving
Code does nothing until the file is saved and run again
computers.why: Source code is just text in storage. A running process keeps using the old version until you save and restart it.

options: A program that reads the commands you type and runs them
The window border around a terminal app
A folder that stores Python packages
A kind of virtual environment for Windows only
terminal.why: The terminal is the window; the shell (bash, zsh, PowerShell) inside it reads each command and runs it.

terminal.q: What does a virtual environment give you?
options: A faster CPU for running scripts
A remote server to run code on
A separate place to install packages for one project
A backup copy of your source files
terminal.why: A venv keeps each project's packages apart, so one project's versions do not break another's.

terminal.q: You type python report.py and get 'No such file or directory', but the file exists. What do you check first?
options: Reinstall Python from scratch
Run pwd and ls to see which folder you are in
Rename the file to report.txt
Restart the computer
terminal.why: The shell looks for relative paths in the current folder. Usually you are just in the wrong directory; cd there or give the full path.

terminal.q: You pip install requests, activate the venv, run your script and get ModuleNotFoundError. Why?
options: requests only works on Linux
The package name must be capitalised
pip needs a reboot before packages load
It was installed before activating, so it went to another Python
terminal.why: pip installs into whichever Python is active. Activate the venv first, then install, so the package lands where your script runs.

terminal.q: A colleague shares a script with the customer's API key typed on line 3. What is the better practice?
options: Keep the key but mark the file read-only
Put the key in a comment so Python ignores it
Shorten the key so it is harder to read
Store the key in an environment variable and read it in code
terminal.why: Secrets in code get shared and committed. Environment variables keep the key out of the file itself.

python1.q: What does a function's return statement do?
options: Prints a value on the screen
Stops the whole program immediately
Sends a value back to the code that called the function
Restarts the function from the top
python1.why: return hands a value back to the caller. print only shows it on screen, and the caller gets nothing.

python1.q: In a traceback, where do you look first?
options: The first line, which names the Python version
The middle lines, which list every import
Any line mentioning a library you installed
The last line, which gives the error type and message
python1.why: Read a traceback from the bottom up. The last line says what went wrong, and the lines above show where.

python1.q: A customer file has quantity '5' and '3' read with input(). Your total prints 53. What is the fix?
options: Convert both with int() before adding
Use * instead of + to combine them
Wrap the result in str()
Add them inside a for loop
python1.why: input() and file reads give strings, and + joins strings. Converting with int() or float() makes + do arithmetic.

python1.q: Your function calc_tax(amount) works when tested alone, but total = calc_tax(100) gives None. What is likely wrong?
options: The parameter needs a default value
The function uses print instead of return
Functions cannot take numbers as inputs
The variable total is a reserved word
python1.why: A function without return gives back None. print shows the value on screen but does not hand it to the caller.

python1.q: Which line would cause a SyntaxError?
options: for x in range(3):
if price > 10:
def total(a, b)
while count < 5:
python1.why: def, if, for and while lines must end with a colon. Missing colons and mixed tabs and spaces are classic beginner errors.

python2.q: Which collection maps keys to values?
options: list
tuple
set
dict
python2.why: A dict stores key and value pairs and looks values up by key. A set holds unique items with no values attached.

python2.q: What does a with open(...) block do for you?
options: It closes the file automatically when the block ends
It converts the file to JSON
It makes the file read-only for other users
It loads the file into a pandas DataFrame
python2.why: The with block closes the file even if an error happens, so data is flushed and the file is not left locked.

python2.q: You compare CSV amounts and '9' > '10' comes out True. What should you do?
options: Sort the rows alphabetically first
Convert the values with float() or int() before comparing
Open the file in 'a' mode instead
Remove the header row
python2.why: The csv module gives strings, and strings compare letter by letter. Convert to numbers before comparing.

python2.q: A customer CSV has a company name 'Brightline, Inc.'. Your parser using line.split(',') shifts every column. Fix?
options: Replace all commas with spaces first
Use more columns in your code
Use the csv module, which handles quoted commas
Switch to reading with json.load
python2.why: Quoted values can contain commas. csv.reader and csv.DictReader handle quoting correctly; a plain split does not.

python2.q: You append daily results to log.csv using open('log.csv', 'w'). Next day only today's rows remain. Why?
options: The with block deletes old rows
CSV files cannot hold more than one day
'w' replaces existing contents; use 'a' to append
You must call file.save() at the end
python2.why: Mode 'w' wipes the file each time it opens. Mode 'a' adds to the end.

options: Encrypts traffic between browser and server
Turns a name like shop.example.com into an IP address
Picks which program on a machine receives a message
Stores web pages so they load faster
internet.why: DNS resolves names to IP addresses. Ports pick the program, and TLS handles encryption.

options: A number that picks which program on a machine you are talking to
The cable that connects a laptop to Wi-Fi
Another name for an IP address
A folder where a server keeps its logs
internet.why: One machine can run many servers, and the port number (443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH) selects one.

internet.q: A customer says 'your service is down' but it works for you. What do you check first?
options: Restart your production servers
Ask them to reinstall their browser
Rewrite the API in a faster language
Whether their machine resolves the name to an IP (DNS)
internet.why: Check layers in order: name, then route and port, then TLS, then HTTP. Often the fault is DNS or a firewall on their side.

internet.q: From a customer VM, the name resolves but a connection to port 443 times out. What is the likely cause?
options: The certificate expired
The server returned a 404
A firewall is blocking that port on the path
The JSON response is malformed
internet.why: A timeout on connect points to a network block. Certificate and HTTP errors only appear after the connection opens.

internet.q: A customer believes HTTPS hides which sites employees visit. What is correct?
options: HTTPS hides the content, but the IP and usually the site name are visible
Yes, HTTPS hides everything about the visit
HTTPS only hides passwords, not page content
HTTPS hides the site name but not the content
internet.why: TLS encrypts the content of the traffic. The network can still see the IP address and usually the site name.

options: A password needed to open the database
The first column in any table
A column that uniquely identifies each row
A column that links to another table
dbbasics.why: A primary key is unique per row. A column that points at another table's key is a foreign key.

dbbasics.q: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Every row from the left table
Only rows that have a match in both tables
Every row from both tables
Rows with no match on either side
dbbasics.why: INNER JOIN keeps only matches. A LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and fills NULL where nothing matches.

dbbasics.q: A customer asks you to fix one misspelled city. You are about to run UPDATE customers SET city='Leeds'. What is missing?
options: A JOIN to the orders table
An ORDER BY clause
A LIMIT of 100 rows
A WHERE clause, or every row gets changed
dbbasics.why: UPDATE and DELETE without WHERE change every row in the table. Always run the matching SELECT first.

dbbasics.q: Your Python script INSERTs rows into SQLite with no errors, but the rows are gone when you reopen the file. Why?
options: SQLite only keeps rows in memory
INSERT needs a primary key value
The table was not indexed
You never called commit() on the connection
dbbasics.why: sqlite3 changes are part of a transaction until you commit. Close without committing and they are discarded.

dbbasics.q: Which is the safe way to use a name typed by a user in a query?
options: f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'"
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s" % name
dbbasics.why: Placeholders let the database treat input as data. Building SQL with string formatting allows SQL injection.

mlbasics.q: In a dataset for predicting house prices, what is the label?
options: The sale price you want to predict
The number of rooms
The algorithm you chose
The row number of each sale
mlbasics.why: The label is the answer to predict. Rooms and size are features, the inputs known at prediction time.

options: Using too little training data to start
Memorising training examples, including noise, so new data goes badly
Training a model for too short a time
Choosing a model that is too simple
mlbasics.why: An overfit model scores well on examples it saw and poorly on new ones. A held-out test set reveals it.

mlbasics.q: A data scientist at Harbor Freight Co. reports 99% accuracy. What do you ask first?
options: Which programming language was used
How long training took
Whether the accuracy is on a held-out test set
Whether the model is a neural network
mlbasics.why: Accuracy on training data looks far better than real life. Only a test set the model never saw shows true performance.

mlbasics.q: A customer wants to calculate tax from a fixed government table. They ask for an ML model. What do you suggest?
options: Train a neural network on past tax bills
Collect a million examples first
Use an LLM to estimate each bill
Write plain rules; the logic is already known
mlbasics.why: ML helps when rules are too fuzzy to write. When the rules are clear and fixed, normal code is cheaper and exact.

mlbasics.q: A teammate says 'the bigger model will always beat logistic regression on our 800 rows.' What is the flaw?
options: On small data, simple models often do as well or better
Logistic regression cannot use numbers
Bigger models never overfit
800 rows is too many for any model
mlbasics.why: Complex models need lots of data and overfit small datasets easily. Try a simple baseline first.

mathbasics.q: What is the dot product of [2, 1, 3] and [1, 0, 2]?
What does softmax do to a model's raw scores?
options: Sorts them from largest to smallest
Rounds them to whole numbers
Removes negative scores
Turns them into probabilities that add up to 1
mathbasics.why: Softmax turns raw scores into values between 0 and 1 that sum to 1, so they can be read as a share of belief.

mathbasics.q: A customer asks how fast your API is. Most calls take 200 ms but a few take 9 s. What do you report?
options: The average latency only
The fastest call you saw
p50 and p95 latency
The total time of all calls
mathbasics.why: Averages hide or get distorted by slow outliers. p50 shows the typical call, p95 shows what the slow tail feels like.

mathbasics.q: You multiply a 2x3 matrix by a vector. How long must the vector be?
options: Any length works
mathbasics.why: Each row is dotted with the vector, so the vector length must match the number of columns, which is 3.

mathbasics.q: A classifier outputs 0.66 for 'fraud'. A manager says 'so it is 66% certain.' What is the trap?
options: Softmax scores are always exactly calibrated
0.66 means the model is 34% certain
Scores above 0.5 are always correct
Softmax gives a score share and is often poorly calibrated
mathbasics.why: Softmax output is a relative share, not a checked probability. Many models are over or under confident.

options: Deletes the log file
Shows the last lines and keeps printing new ones as they arrive
Shows the first 10 lines only
Opens the log in a text editor
linux.why: tail -f follows the file live, which is the fastest way to watch what a service is doing.

linux.q: In SSH key authentication, which key stays on your laptop?
options: The private key
The public key
Both keys, and neither goes to the server
Neither; keys live in /etc on the server
linux.why: The private key never leaves your machine. The public key goes into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server.

linux.q: A pipeline on a customer server gets 'Permission denied' writing to /data/out. What do you do first?
options: Run chmod 777 on /data/out
Delete the folder and recreate it
Check the folder's owner and permissions with ls -l
Reboot the server
linux.why: Find out who owns it and what is allowed, then grant only what is needed. chmod 777 lets every user change the files.

linux.q: A stuck Python worker needs to stop. What should you try first?
options: kill -9 on its PID
Delete the script file
Unplug the network
kill (SIGTERM) so it can clean up
linux.why: SIGTERM lets the program finish writes and exit cleanly. kill -9 is a last resort because it stops it instantly.

linux.q: Which habit leaks secrets on a shared customer server?
options: Reading keys from environment variables
Pasting an API key directly into a curl command
Storing keys in a secret manager
Using ssh-agent for your private key
linux.why: Commands typed in the shell are saved to history in plain text, so anyone who reads it gets the key.

frontend.q: What is the role of CSS?
options: It describes how the page looks
It describes the page's content and structure
It makes the page respond to clicks
It stores data on the server
frontend.why: HTML is structure, CSS is appearance, and JavaScript is behaviour.

frontend.q: What does TypeScript add to JavaScript?
options: Faster execution in the browser
A built-in database
Type checks that catch mistakes before the code runs
Automatic page styling
frontend.why: TypeScript checks types while you write, so errors like reading the wrong field show up before a customer sees them.

frontend.q: Your demo calls the customer's API from the browser and the console shows a CORS error. What does it mean?
options: The API is down
The API key is wrong
The JSON is malformed
The server does not allow requests from your page's origin
frontend.why: CORS is the browser enforcing the server's rules about which origins may call it. Fix it on the server or call from a backend.

frontend.q: You have two days to show Nimbus Logistics a document-search demo. What do you prioritise?
options: A custom component library
Pixel-perfect design and animations
A full React app with routing and auth
A working flow on their real data, even with plain styling
frontend.why: A demo must answer the customer's real question. Streamlit or a simple page with their data beats polish on fake data.

frontend.q: A demo page has fetch() calls to an LLM with the API key in the JavaScript. What is wrong?
options: fetch cannot call LLM APIs
Anyone can open developer tools and copy the key
The key will expire faster in a browser
JavaScript cannot send headers
frontend.why: Anything in browser code is visible to the user. Keep keys on a backend that calls the model for the page.

oop.q: What is a class in Python?
options: A single value stored in a variable
A file that holds several functions
A blueprint that defines data and methods for objects
A loop that runs over a list
oop.why: A class describes what data an object holds and what it can do. Each object made from it is an instance.

options: It sets up a new object's starting attributes
It deletes an object when finished
It imports the class into another file
It prints the object nicely
oop.why: __init__ runs when you create an instance and stores its starting values on self.

oop.q: You connect to three customer CRMs with different APIs. How do you keep pipeline code simple?
options: Copy the pipeline three times, one per CRM
Put all three APIs into one giant if/elif function
Ask the customers to change their APIs
Write one class per CRM with the same methods, like get_contacts()
oop.why: A shared interface lets the pipeline call get_contacts() without caring which CRM it is. Each class hides its own quirks.

oop.q: A teammate built Invoice(Order), a subclass, only to reuse one helper function. What do you suggest?
options: Add two more levels of inheritance
Use composition or a plain function instead
Make every class inherit from Invoice
Remove all methods from Order
oop.why: Inheritance means 'is a'. An invoice is not an order, so sharing a helper through composition or a function is cleaner.

oop.q: What goes wrong in: def __init__(self, tags=[]): self.tags = tags?
options: All instances share the same list object
Lists cannot be attributes
self is missing from the parameters
The class cannot be instantiated
oop.why: A mutable default is created once and shared by every call. Use tags=None and create a new list inside.

asyncpy.q: What does await do inside an async function?
options: Runs the code on a new CPU core
Pauses this task until the result is ready, letting others run
Blocks the whole program until done
Retries the call if it fails
asyncpy.why: await hands control back to the event loop while waiting, so other tasks can make progress in the meantime.

asyncpy.q: Which kind of work benefits most from asyncio?
options: Heavy number crunching on one big array
Resizing thousands of images in memory
Many network calls that spend time waiting
Sorting a huge list
asyncpy.why: Async helps when code waits on I/O like HTTP calls. CPU-heavy work needs processes, not async.

asyncpy.q: You must fetch 2,000 records one API call each from a slow customer API. What speeds this up safely?
options: Fire all 2,000 at once with no limit
Loop over them one by one with requests
Run calls concurrently with asyncio.gather and a semaphore limit
Add time.sleep between calls
asyncpy.why: Concurrency hides waiting time, and a semaphore caps parallel calls so you do not overload their API or hit rate limits.

asyncpy.q: Inside an async function, a teammate calls time.sleep(5) and requests.get(). What happens?
options: Nothing; they are async automatically
Python raises a SyntaxError
The calls run faster than usual
They block the event loop, so all other tasks freeze
asyncpy.why: Blocking calls stop the whole loop. Use await asyncio.sleep and an async HTTP client such as httpx or aiohttp.

asyncpy.q: Your code calls fetch_page(1) without await and gets a coroutine object instead of data. Why?
options: Calling an async function only creates a coroutine; you must await it
The API returned an error
fetch_page needs to be a class
Coroutines only work in Jupyter
asyncpy.why: An async function returns a coroutine that does nothing until awaited or scheduled as a task.

stats.q: What does the median tell you?
options: The most common value
The sum divided by the count
The middle value when data is sorted
The gap between highest and lowest
stats.why: Half the values are below the median and half above. Unlike the mean, it barely moves with outliers.

options: The chance the result is important for the business
How likely data this extreme is if there were no real effect
The probability the hypothesis is true
The size of the difference between groups
stats.why: A p-value assumes no effect and asks how surprising the data would be. It is not the chance your idea is right.

stats.q: A customer says ice cream sales and drownings rise together, so ice cream is dangerous. What do you point out?
options: Correlation is strong, so causation is proven
The data must be wrong
Drownings cause ice cream sales
A third factor, hot weather, may drive both
stats.why: Correlation is not causation. A hidden confounder such as temperature can move both numbers.

stats.q: Kestrel Retail ran an A/B test with 40 users per group and wants to ship. What do you check first?
options: Whether the sample is big enough to trust the difference
Which button colour looks nicer
Whether the test ran on a weekday
How many engineers built each version
stats.why: Tiny samples give noisy results. Check sample size and confidence intervals before calling a winner.

stats.q: A report says 'average deal size is $50k' but most deals are $5k and two are $2M. What is the trap?
options: The mean is always the best summary
Outliers pull the mean far above the typical deal
The median would be even higher
Deal sizes cannot be averaged
stats.why: A few extreme values drag the mean. Report the median, and say the outliers exist.

genesis.q: What best describes a Forward Deployed Engineer?
options: A salesperson who gives product demos
A consultant who writes reports and bills hours
An engineer who ships production code inside one customer and feeds lessons to the product
A support agent who answers tickets
genesis.why: FDEs build and deploy real code on the vendor's platform at the customer, and push repeated needs back into the product.

genesis.q: In the Echo and Delta split, what does the Echo own?
options: Building the core product roadmap alone
Writing the data pipelines
Running the cloud infrastructure
Understanding the customer's organisation, problem and success metric
genesis.why: The Echo, or Deployment Strategist, frames the problem and manages the relationship. The Deltas build.

genesis.q: At Orion Freight you hand-build the same CSV connector for the third customer in a row. What do you do?
options: Keep building it by hand each time
Charge the customer extra for it
Stop supporting CSV files
Log it as a repeated gap and push it to the product team
genesis.why: Closing the loop turns repeated field work into product features, so each deployment needs less custom work.

genesis.q: A customer sends a vague request: 'make our planning smarter.' Acting as a human API, what do you do?
options: Forward the message to the product team as a ticket
Translate it into a concrete problem and metric, then build
Wait until they write a full requirements document
Start training a large model right away
genesis.why: A human API translates, filters and builds. Just relaying requests turns you into a ticket router.

genesis.q: Which sign shows an FDE team slipping into being a consultancy?
options: Every deployment stays custom and nothing reaches the product
FDEs spend most of their time writing code
Deployments get faster over time
The product gains connectors from field work
genesis.why: The model pays off only when field work becomes product. Otherwise it is software with consulting attached.

options: Revenue from new customers this year
Profit after all costs are paid
How revenue from existing customers changes, counting expansion, contraction and churn
The number of customers who renewed
slg.why: NRR = (starting ARR + expansion - contraction - churn) / starting ARR. Above 100% means the base grows without new logos.

slg.q: Why do FDE-heavy companies often have lower gross margin?
options: Engineer time on customer work adds to cost of goods sold
They charge lower prices
Cloud hosting is free for pure software firms
They pay no sales commissions
slg.why: Putting engineers on deployments raises COGS. The company trades that margin for a moat of deep, sticky deployments.

slg.q: Your first deployment at Pinecrest Health works. How do you help drive expansion?
options: Add as many features as possible to the first workflow
Wait for leadership to ask for more
Offer discounts to the current team
Show a clear win metric and find the next team with a similar problem
slg.why: Land and expand: one visible win with a metric leaders care about, then make it easy for the next team to start.

slg.q: Leadership asks if SLG is working. Which two numbers do you track?
options: Number of FDEs and office locations
FDE hours per new deployment and NRR
Website traffic and sign-ups
Lines of code and bugs fixed
slg.why: You want FDE hours per deployment going down as work becomes product, and NRR staying high.

slg.q: A founder says 'lower margin is fine forever, FDEs are our product.' What is the problem?
options: NRR does not matter for SLG
FDEs always raise gross margin
If deployments stay bespoke, margins never improve
Switching costs make margin irrelevant
slg.why: The margin cost is only worth it if field work becomes product and hours per deployment fall.

http.q: What does a 429 status code mean?
options: Not found
Server crashed
Too many requests; slow down
Request succeeded
http.why: 429 means you hit a rate limit. Wait, often per the Retry-After header, then retry.

http.q: Which HTTP method is normally used to read data without changing it?
options: POST
GET
PUT
DELETE
http.why: GET reads. POST creates, PUT replaces, DELETE removes.

http.q: A customer's API returns 401 from your pipeline. What do you check first?
options: Whether the token is missing, wrong or expired
Whether the server is overloaded
Whether your JSON body has a typo
Whether the URL uses HTTP instead of HTTPS
http.why: 401 means the server does not accept your credentials. A 429 would mean wait, and a 400 would mean fix the request.

http.q: Your pipeline fails against a customer API and you are unsure why. What is a good first step?
options: Rewrite the pipeline in another language
Ask the customer to change their API
Add more retries and hope it passes
Reproduce the call with curl to isolate the problem
http.why: curl removes your code from the picture. If curl fails too, the issue is auth, network or the API, not your pipeline.

http.q: You pull a customer's orders and report 'you have exactly 100 orders.' What likely went wrong?
options: You only read the first page of results
The API only stores 100 orders
JSON cannot hold more than 100 items
Your token limits you to 100 rows forever
http.why: APIs return data in pages. Loop until there are no more pages, or you will under-count.

options: Saves a commit to the remote
Creates a new branch
Copies a file's current state into the staging area
Downloads the latest changes
git.why: git add stages changes. git commit then saves exactly what is staged.

git.q: You pushed a bad commit to a shared branch. What is the safe way to undo it?
options: Edit the files and never commit
git reset --hard and force-push
Delete the repository and clone again
git revert, which adds a new commit undoing it
git.why: revert keeps history intact for everyone. Rewriting shared history can erase teammates' work.

git.q: You accidentally committed a .env file with a customer's API key and pushed it. What do you do?
options: Delete the file in a new commit and move on
Make the repo private
Rename the file to .env.old
Rotate the key, then remove the file and add .env to .gitignore
git.why: Git history keeps the old commit, so the key is exposed. Rotating it is the only real fix.

git.q: After a week of work you have one PR mixing a new connector, a refactor and bug fixes. Reviewers stall. Better?
options: Ask reviewers to approve without reading
Split it into smaller focused pull requests
Merge it yourself without review
Add more comments to the giant PR
git.why: Small PRs with one purpose are easier to review properly and safer to merge or roll back.

git.q: A teammate's push was rejected, so they plan git push --force on main. What is the risk?
options: It is always safe on main
It only affects their local copy
It can erase commits other people already pushed
Git will merge automatically
git.why: Force-pushing overwrites the remote branch. Pull and merge or rebase instead.

tdd.q: What is the order of the TDD loop?
options: Green, red, refactor
Refactor, red, green
Red, refactor, green
Red, green, refactor
tdd.why: Write a failing test (red), make it pass simply (green), then clean up the code (refactor) while tests stay green.

options: A function that prepares something a test needs
A test that always passes
A tool that measures code coverage
A file listing CI settings
tdd.why: Fixtures set up sample data, temp files or connections, and pytest passes them to tests that name them as arguments.

tdd.q: You are writing an ingestion job for a customer API. Which tests are most valuable first?
options: Tests for a perfectly clean response only
Tests for 429, 500, timeout and malformed records
Tests that check the CSS of the dashboard
Tests that count lines of code
tdd.why: Failure paths break pipelines in production. Mock those responses so you can test them on demand.

tdd.q: Your unit tests call the customer's live API and often fail randomly. What do you change?
options: Mock the API in unit tests; keep a few separate integration tests
Run the tests more times until they pass
Delete the flaky tests
Increase the timeout to 5 minutes
tdd.why: Live calls are slow, flaky and can change real data. Unit tests should use fakes.

tdd.q: A test mocks the parser, the API and the writer, then asserts the mock returned what it was told. What is wrong?
options: It needs more fixtures
It is too fast
It checks only the mock and proves nothing about your code
It should use unittest instead of pytest
tdd.why: Over-mocking tests the fake. Mock only the external boundary and let your real logic run.

bigo.q: Checking x in a Python set is typically what complexity?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
bigo.why: Sets and dicts use a hash table, so lookups jump straight to the item. x in a list is O(n).

bigo.q: A function does 3n + 50 steps. What is its Big-O?
options: O(n)
bigo.why: Big-O drops constants and small terms, keeping only how work grows with n.

bigo.q: A dedupe script checks each of 1 million rows against a list of seen IDs and runs for hours. What is the fix?
options: Use a faster laptop
Store seen IDs in a set instead of a list
Split the file into 10 parts
Sort the list after every row
bigo.why: Membership in a list is O(n), making the whole job O(n^2). A set makes each check O(1).

bigo.q: Your code gets 5,000 order IDs, then calls the API once per order for details. It is very slow. Why?
options: The API returns too much JSON
Python loops are always slow
It is the N+1 problem; fetch details in bulk
The order IDs are not sorted
bigo.why: One call per item multiplies network round trips by n. Use a batch endpoint or bulk query.

bigo.q: A teammate tested a join on 100 rows, it ran in 0.1 s, so they shipped it. What is the trap?
options: Small tests hide an O(n^2) loop that explodes on 1 million rows
100 rows is too many for a test
0.1 s means the code is O(1)
Joins always run in constant time
bigo.why: Quadratic work looks fast on tiny data. Estimate growth or test at realistic size.

options: Retrying immediately as many times as possible
Stopping after the first failure
Waiting longer after each failure, like 1, 2, 4, 8 seconds
Sending requests in random order
resilient.why: Backing off gives a struggling server time to recover. Adding jitter spreads retries so clients do not stampede.

options: A place that stores failed records with the reason, for later replay
A list of deleted users
A queue that drops bad records forever
A cache of successful API responses
resilient.why: Nothing is thrown away. You can report data quality issues and replay records after a fix.

resilient.q: Your ingestion job crashes halfway through 400 pages of a customer API. What design lets it resume safely?
options: Start from page 1 every time
Save a checkpoint (cursor) and use idempotent writes
Download everything into memory first
Skip the pages that failed
resilient.why: A checkpoint lets you restart where you stopped, and idempotent writes mean re-processing a page does no harm.

resilient.q: A customer API sometimes hangs for minutes and your worker freezes. What is missing?
options: A bigger server
More logging lines
A faster JSON parser
A timeout on every HTTP call
resilient.why: Without a timeout, one stuck request can hold a worker forever. Set one and treat it as a retryable error.

resilient.q: Your retry loop retries every error, including 400 Bad Request, five times. What is the mistake?
options: 400 means the server is overloaded
400 should be retried ten times
Retries should only happen on 200
400 means the request is wrong; retrying will not fix it
resilient.why: Retry transient errors like 429, 5xx and timeouts. A 400 needs a code or data fix.

sql.q: In logical order, which clause runs before SELECT?
options: ORDER BY
LIMIT
WHERE
None; SELECT always runs first
sql.why: Logical order is FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. So WHERE cannot use a SELECT alias.

sql.q: How do you correctly find rows where email is missing?
options: WHERE email = NULL
WHERE email IS NULL
WHERE email = ''
WHERE email == NULL
sql.why: Any comparison with NULL returns unknown, which WHERE treats as false. Use IS NULL.

sql.q: A customer says your revenue total is 3x too high after joining orders to order_items. What do you check first?
options: Row counts before and after the join to spot fan-out
Whether the database needs more RAM
Whether SUM is spelled correctly
The ORDER BY clause
sql.why: Joining one-to-many repeats each order per item, so summing order totals triples them. Check the grain.

sql.q: A customer wants each sale shown with that rep's running total, keeping every row. What do you use?
options: GROUP BY rep
A subquery with DISTINCT
A HAVING clause
SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY rep ORDER BY date)
sql.why: A window function adds a column without collapsing rows. GROUP BY would return one row per rep.

sql.q: A query filters AVG(amount) > 100 inside WHERE and errors. What is the mistake?
options: AVG is not allowed in SQL
Filters on aggregates belong in HAVING
WHERE must come after GROUP BY
Amounts must be cast to text first
sql.why: WHERE runs before grouping, so aggregates do not exist yet. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

planner.q: What does the query planner do?
options: Checks your SQL for spelling mistakes only
Stores data in tables
Chooses how to fetch data, such as scan or index, based on estimated cost
Backs up the database nightly
planner.why: The planner compares candidate plans and picks the cheapest by its estimates. The executor then runs it.

planner.q: How do you read an EXPLAIN plan tree?
options: From the most indented line upward
From the top line downward
Only the last line matters
Alphabetically by node name
planner.why: Innermost nodes run first and feed their parents, so start at the deepest indentation.

planner.q: A report query at Tidewater Bank filters on customer_id and sorts by created_at. It is slow. What do you try?
options: An index on (created_at, customer_id)
Two separate hash indexes
Removing the ORDER BY for the customer
A composite index on (customer_id, created_at)
planner.why: Equality column first, then the sort or range column, lets a B-tree jump to the customer and read rows already sorted.

planner.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated rows 10 but actual rows 2,000,000. What does this suggest?
options: The query has a syntax error
Table statistics are stale; run ANALYZE
The server is out of disk space
The index is too big
planner.why: Bad estimates lead to bad plans. Refreshing statistics often fixes it.

planner.q: A teammate wants to add an index on every column of a busy orders table 'to be safe.' What is the trap?
options: Postgres only allows one index per table
Indexes are free and always help
Every index slows writes and uses space
Indexes only work on text columns
planner.why: Each insert and update must maintain every index. Add indexes that real queries need.

options: A key that must be encrypted
The first column of every table
A column that points to the primary key of another table
A key used only in NoSQL databases
normalize.why: Foreign keys link tables, such as orders.customer_id pointing to customers.id.

normalize.q: What does first normal form (1NF) require?
options: Each column holds a single value, not a list
Every table has at least three columns
No table has a foreign key
All data sits in one table
normalize.why: A cell like 'SKU1, SKU2, SKU3' breaks 1NF. Split repeating values into their own rows or table.

normalize.q: Crescent Books sends an orders sheet with customer address repeated on every row. A customer moves. What happens?
options: Nothing; the sheet updates itself
Only the first row needs changing
Addresses cannot change in spreadsheets
You must update many rows and may miss some
normalize.why: Repeated facts drift out of sync. Normalizing puts the address in one customers row.

normalize.q: You are designing a customers table. Which is the best primary key?
options: The customer's email address
A surrogate id, with email kept unique
The customer's full name
The customer's phone number
normalize.why: Emails and names can change or repeat. A stable surrogate id avoids breaking every link when they do.

normalize.q: A teammate loads the customer's messy sheet straight into one wide table and builds the app on it. What is the risk?
options: Duplicated facts will conflict and updates will miss rows
Wide tables cannot be queried
The database will reject the load
Joins become impossible forever
normalize.why: Building on unnormalized data bakes in duplication. Model the entities first, then load.

options: Every query runs in under a second
All changes in a transaction happen, or none do
Data is copied to many servers
Only one user can connect at a time
acid.why: Atomicity is all or nothing. If one step fails, ROLLBACK undoes the rest.

options: By keeping everything in RAM
By refusing concurrent writes
By writing changes to a write-ahead log on disk before COMMIT returns
By emailing a backup each night
acid.why: Once COMMIT returns, the change is in the WAL on disk, so it survives a crash.

acid.q: A payment moves money between two accounts, and the app crashed after the debit only. What should the code have done?
options: Log the error and continue
Run the credit first next time
Add a retry around the debit
Put both updates in one transaction with BEGIN and COMMIT
acid.why: Wrapping both updates in one transaction means a crash leaves neither applied, not half.

acid.q: Two workers read stock=5, each subtract 1, and write 4. One sale was lost. What is a fix?
options: Run the workers on different days
Add more RAM
Use a bigger integer type
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or an atomic UPDATE stock = stock - 1
acid.why: Read-modify-write races lose updates. Lock the row or let the database do the math in one statement.

acid.q: A developer checks 'email must be unique' only in app code, not the schema. What is the trap?
options: Concurrent requests can still insert duplicates
App checks are always enough
Constraints make inserts impossible
UNIQUE only works on numbers
acid.why: Two requests can pass the app check at the same time. A UNIQUE constraint makes the database enforce the rule.

spark.q: What is a partition in Spark?
options: A chunk of the dataset processed in parallel
A separate Spark cluster
A backup copy of a table
A type of join
spark.why: Spark splits data into partitions, and executors process them in parallel.

spark.q: When does a Spark transformation like filter actually run?
options: Immediately when you write it
Only when an action like count or write is called
Every time you save the notebook
Never; filters are ignored
spark.why: Transformations are lazy. Spark builds a plan and runs it only when an action asks for a result.

spark.q: You join a 2 TB events table to a 5 MB country lookup and the job is slow. What do you try?
options: Increase the shuffle partitions to 10,000
Collect the big table to the driver
Broadcast the small table so the big one does not shuffle
Convert both tables to CSV
spark.why: A broadcast join copies the small side to every executor, so the huge table never moves across the network.

spark.q: One task in a join runs for an hour while others finish in a minute. What is the likely cause?
options: The cluster has too many executors
Parquet files are too small
The driver is out of disk
Data skew: one key has far more rows than others
spark.why: A hot key sends most rows to one task. Salting the key or broadcast joins spread the work.

spark.q: A notebook calls df.collect() on a 500 GB DataFrame and crashes. What is the mistake?
options: The DataFrame needed caching first
collect() only works on CSV
collect() pulls all data to the driver, which runs out of memory
The cluster has too few partitions
spark.why: collect brings every row to one machine. Write results out, or use take or show for a sample.

etl.q: What is a watermark in extraction?
options: A logo stamped on exported files
A saved high point, like last updated_at, to pull only new rows
A full copy of every row
An encryption key for the source
etl.why: Watermarks enable incremental loads, so you avoid copying a 200 million row table every night.

etl.q: What does idempotent mean for a pipeline job?
options: It runs faster the second time
It never fails
Running it twice gives the same result as once
It only runs once a day
etl.why: Pipelines get retried. Idempotent loads, like MERGE on a key, do not create duplicates on rerun.

etl.q: A transformation bug corrupted last week's clean tables at Maple Grocers. What lets you recover without the customer?
options: Having landed the raw extracted data unchanged
Asking the customer to export again
Restoring your laptop from backup
Editing the rows by hand
etl.why: Keeping a raw layer means you fix the code and rerun over the raw data.

etl.q: A business user asks why yesterday's dashboard is empty. What pipeline feature should have caught it?
options: A bigger warehouse
More columns in the source
A faster orchestrator
Freshness and row-count data quality tests
etl.why: Tests after each step catch stale or missing data before users or AI agents see it.

etl.q: A nightly job uses plain INSERT. It failed halfway, was retried, and totals doubled. What is the fix?
options: Use MERGE or delete-then-insert on a key so reruns are safe
Never retry failed jobs
Run the job twice as often
Add an index on the target table
etl.why: Appending on retry creates duplicates. An idempotent load keyed on a unique id gives the same result each run.

warehouse.q: Why is columnar storage fast for analytics?
options: It stores each row together on disk
Queries read only the columns they need, and columns compress well
It keeps everything in RAM
It disables indexes
warehouse.why: Analytic queries touch a few columns across many rows. Column stores skip the rest and compress similar values.

warehouse.q: In a star schema, what is a fact table?
options: A table of descriptive attributes like product name
A lookup of country codes
A log of schema changes
One row per business event with numeric measures and keys
warehouse.why: Facts hold events and measures. Dimensions around them describe who, what, where and when.

warehouse.q: Summit Outdoor wants 3-year sales dashboards and plans to query their live order database. What do you advise?
options: Turn off transactions to speed it up
Add more dashboards to the live database
Run the queries only at lunchtime
Copy data into a warehouse so analytics does not slow the live app
warehouse.why: Heavy scans on the OLTP database hurt the live application. A warehouse is built for this workload.

warehouse.q: A customer's warehouse bill jumped after analysts started using SELECT * on a 300-column table. Why?
options: SELECT * is blocked on warehouses
Wide tables are always free
Per-byte pricing charges for every column scanned
SELECT * forces a full backup
warehouse.why: Warehouses with on-demand pricing, such as BigQuery, bill by bytes scanned, and in a column store SELECT * scans every column. Compute-billed warehouses like Snowflake also cost more because the scan takes longer. Select only the columns you need.

warehouse.q: Revenue doubled after joining sales to a Type 2 customer dimension on customer_id only. What was missed?
options: A date condition matching the valid version of each customer
A GROUP BY on product
A LEFT JOIN instead of INNER
A DISTINCT on the fact table
warehouse.why: Type 2 keeps several rows per customer. Without a validity date filter each fact matches every version.
